analysis.one_liner: Widens the Medicare drug price negotiation exemption for rare-disease drugs.
analysis.headline: Introduced May 22, 2025 with one Democratic cosponsor and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has seen no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare's Drug Price Negotiation Program lets the government negotiate lower prices for expensive drugs once they have been on the market for 7 years (regular drugs) or 11 years (biologics). Drugs approved to treat a single rare disease are already exempt. This bill widens that exemption in two ways: drugs approved to treat more than one rare disease would be exempt too, and any years a drug spent with a rare-disease "orphan" designation would not count toward the waiting clock — so a drug's countdown to price negotiation could be stretched out or paused entirely.
analysis.who_benefits: Manufacturers of rare-disease drugs, and makers of widely used drugs that hold or could pick up an orphan designation. They would keep charging Medicare higher prices for longer, free from negotiated rates. Supporters argue the carve-out keeps development worthwhile for drugs with very small patient populations.

how_it_helps.text: The bill excludes any period a drug carried an orphan-drug designation from the 7-year (drugs) or 11-year (biologics) waiting period before Medicare can negotiate its price, so makers can pause or extend the countdown. [S2][S3]
It also extends the full negotiation exemption to drugs approved to treat more than one rare disease or condition, where current law covers only single-rare-disease drugs. [S2][S3]

analysis.who_pays: Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers. When drugs stay outside negotiation, Medicare pays more, and those costs flow into premiums, cost-sharing, and the federal budget.

drawbacks.text: Drugs approved for multiple rare diseases can still have large Medicare markets; exempting them from negotiation means Medicare pays unregulated prices for drugs that are no longer small-market orphans. [S2][S3]

The clock exclusion gives drug makers a roadmap to delay negotiation on any drug by obtaining or holding an orphan designation, even for drugs also used to treat common conditions, raising costs for patients with ordinary diseases whose drugs are shielded. [S2][S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The narrow orphan exemption in current law serves a defensible purpose: a drug for a truly tiny patient population may never earn back its development costs at negotiated prices. This bill goes well past that rationale. It shields multi-rare-disease drugs and lets makers pause the negotiation clock with orphan designations, protecting revenue on drugs with real Medicare sales. The cost lands on Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers in the form of higher drug spending; the benefit flows to drug manufacturers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which has taken no further action on it, so it simply sits there with the negotiation program's current rules unchanged.

narrative.text: Senator John Barrasso introduced the ORPHAN Cures Act on May 22, 2025, with Senator Martin Heinrich as cosponsor. [S1][S4]
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance, the committee with jurisdiction over Medicare. [S5]
As of the latest action history, no markup, hearing, or vote has been scheduled, and the Congress remains in session. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has won or lost: the bill has not moved, and Medicare's current negotiation rules — including the narrower single-rare-disease orphan exemption that already benefits drug makers — remain the law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, no one; bill sits in committee

for.name: John Barrasso
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded its referral to the Finance Committee.

for.name: Martin Heinrich
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only Democratic support in the Senate.

for.name: Rare-disease drug manufacturers and allied rare-disease foundations
for.role: Industry coalition promoting the ORPHAN Cures Act
for.what_they_did: Publicly promoted the bill and the broader orphan-drug carve-out during the 2025 Medicare negotiation fight.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only support in the record is a Republican sponsor (Barrasso) paired with a single Democratic cosponsor (Heinrich, 1 of 45 Senate Democrats); no one is recorded in opposition because the bill never advanced. [S4]

industries.note: The bill exempts their products from Medicare price negotiation even when a drug treats several rare diseases and has substantial Medicare sales. Drug prices not subject to negotiation stay higher, and the cost shows up in Medicare premiums and federal spending.

industries.industry: Brand-name drug makers with large Medicare markets
industries.note: The clock exclusion lets any manufacturer extend the years before Medicare can negotiate a drug's price by obtaining an orphan designation, a way to keep unregulated pricing on drugs used for common conditions too.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Finance Committee with one cosponsor and no scheduled action. Most Senate bills referred to committee never get a markup or floor vote. The more likely path for provisions like this is attachment to a larger package, such as a health or budget bill, where a narrow orphan-drug exemption can pass with little attention; standalone, it is likely to remain pending through the Congress.
